tasks.prompt: Order the steps for an annual pressure zone review for a foothills city system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one pressure zone, from data review to the approved action list.

cards.label: Review the zone map, boundary valves and pressure records for the past year
Compare recorded high and low pressures with the zone target range
Identify streets with repeated low pressure or high pressure complaints
Inspect the boundary valves and the pressure reducing valve station records
Rank corrective actions by risk to customers and water quality
Present the review and the action list to the supervisor for approval

tasks.explanation: Annual review starts from records so field work targets real problems. Boundary and reducing valve condition explain many pressure patterns, actions are ranked before approval, and the approved list becomes the work plan.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a pressure reducing valve maintenance program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program setup for all reducing valve stations in the system.

cards.label: Inventory every pressure reducing valve station and record its zone and setpoint
Classify stations by size, age and consequence of failure
Set an inspection interval for each class of station
Create a standard station check sheet covering pressures, strainer and pilot lines
Schedule the first round of inspections and assign crews
File the program and review dates in the maintenance system

tasks.explanation: A program needs a complete inventory before intervals can be set fairly. Classification by consequence focuses effort where failure hurts most, a standard sheet keeps checks consistent, and scheduling plus filing makes the program repeatable.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a boundary valve integrity program between two pressure zones.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all normally closed boundary valves between the upper and lower zones.

cards.label: List every boundary valve from the system map and field verify its location
Record the as found position and normal position for each valve
Exercise each valve and compare opening and closing turn counts
Repair or schedule replacement for any valve that passes or will not operate
Update the zone map where field positions differ from the record
Report program completion and remaining deficiencies to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Boundary valves only protect zone separation if they truly close and are left in the normal position. Field verification corrects the map, exercising proves operability, and deficiencies are repaired or reported rather than assumed away.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for tying a new subdivision into an existing pressure zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one new subdivision main connecting to the existing zone.

cards.label: Confirm the subdivision design pressures match the receiving zone range
Verify the tie in valves and the pressure at the connection point
Flush and disinfect the new main under the utility procedure
Collect and review the required water quality samples
Open the tie in valves slowly and monitor zone pressures during filling
Update the zone map and add the new mains and valves to the inventory

tasks.explanation: Design pressures must match the zone before any connection is made. The new main is proven clean before it is opened to customers, filling is monitored for pressure effects, and records are updated so the zone stays manageable.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for investigating a cluster of low pressure complaints in one zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a neighbourhood cluster of low pressure reports over one week.

cards.label: Map the complaint addresses and the times the low pressure was noticed
Check zone pressure records and pump and tank levels for those times
Deploy temporary pressure loggers at the cluster and at the zone inlet
Compare logger results to find where pressure is lost in the zone
Inspect the suspected valves, reducing valve or restriction found
Report the cause and the corrective action to the supervisor and customers

tasks.explanation: Complaint mapping shows whether the problem is local or zone wide. Loggers at the inlet and in the cluster separate a supply problem from a distribution restriction, and inspection follows the evidence rather than guessing.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reducing excessive night pressures in a lower pressure zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one lower zone where night pressures exceed the target range.

cards.label: Confirm the high night pressures with logger records over several nights
Check the reducing valve setpoint and its recorded maintenance history
Inspect the reducing valve pilot system and strainer for faults
Adjust the setpoint in small steps and monitor downstream pressure after each step
Check leakage and burst history to confirm the benefit of the change
Record the new setpoint and add the station to closer monitoring

tasks.explanation: Night pressures are confirmed with data before any adjustment. Pilot and strainer faults are corrected first, setpoint changes are made gradually with monitoring, and the new setting is recorded so the change is controlled.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a seasonal pressure logging program across all zones.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: logger deployment for a spring pressure study.

cards.label: Select logging points that represent inlets, high points and low points in each zone
Calibrate and time synchronize all loggers before deployment
Install loggers and record the exact location and start time for each
Retrieve loggers after the planned logging period and download the data
Analyse minimum, average and maximum pressures by zone
File the study report and flag zones outside the target range for action

tasks.explanation: Representative points and synchronized clocks make zone comparisons valid. Analysis by zone turns raw traces into decisions, and flagging out of range zones closes the loop from measurement to action.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning a new pressure zone split in a growing hillside area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: planning stage only, from demand review to the approved split concept.

cards.label: Review growth, demands and pressure complaints in the hillside area
Identify the elevation band where a separate zone would hold pressures in range
Locate candidate boundary streets and valves for the new zone line
Assess storage and pumping changes the split would require
Model the concept pressures for the high and low sides of the split
Present the split concept and its effects to management for approval

tasks.explanation: A split is justified by growth and pressure evidence, not by map neatness. The elevation band defines the boundary, storage and pumping effects must be understood before approval, and modelling checks the concept before design money is spent.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing fire flow availability by pressure zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual fire flow review using hydrant test results.

cards.label: Collect the latest hydrant flow test results for each zone
Compare available flows with the fire protection needs identified for each area
List hydrants and streets where available flow is below the need
Check whether low results follow low zone pressure, small mains or closed valves
Rank improvement options for the deficient areas
Share the review with the fire department and file it in the zone records

tasks.explanation: Flow results only matter when compared with the protection need for each area. Checking valves and pressures separates simple fixes from capital needs, ranking guides investment, and sharing the review keeps fire planning aligned.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adjusting zone operations for peak summer demand in a prairie city.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: seasonal operating change for high irrigation demand.

cards.label: Review last summer peak demands and the lowest zone pressures recorded
Confirm tank operating levels and pump capacity for the coming peak
Adjust reducing valve and pump control settings for the seasonal plan
Notify operators and dispatch of the seasonal settings and trigger points
Monitor zone pressures daily during the first peak week
Restore normal settings after the peak and record what was learned

tasks.explanation: Last summer data sets the plan, capacity is confirmed before settings change, and all shifts work from the same trigger points. Daily monitoring in the first peak week catches problems early, and restoring settings with notes prepares the next season.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for maintaining thawing equipment readiness through winter.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program for electric and hot water thaw units.

cards.label: Inventory thaw units and record their location and condition at winter start
Test each unit under load and repair or replace failed units
Stock cables, hoses, fittings and safety gear with each unit
Train or refresh operators on the approved thaw methods for each pipe material
Track unit use and any damage after each deployment
Service units at winter end and record lessons for next season stocking

tasks.explanation: Thaw equipment fails when it is stored untested, so units are proven under load before they are needed. Gear stocked with the unit prevents night delays, material specific training prevents pipe damage during thawing, and end of season service closes the loop.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a district metered area for water loss control.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one district metered area in a residential district.

cards.label: Define the district boundary using valves that can isolate the area
Install or verify the district inlet meter and a data logger
Close and tag boundary valves and prove the district is discrete by a pressure check
Record the customer count and the main lengths inside the district
Start routine night flow logging for the district
Compare the first month night flows with the expected legitimate night use

tasks.explanation: A district must be provably discrete before its night flow means anything. The inlet meter measures everything entering, customer and main data give context, and only then can night flow be judged against legitimate use.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for analysing minimum night flow in a district metered area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one month of night flow data for one district.

cards.label: Download the inlet flow and pressure data for the month
Identify the minimum night flow period on typical nights
Subtract the assessed legitimate night use by customers
Convert the remaining flow to a leakage rate for the district
Compare the leakage rate with the district target and with other districts
Flag the district for leak detection if leakage exceeds the target

tasks.explanation: Night flow analysis works because legitimate use is lowest and steadiest at night. Subtracting assessed night use leaves leakage, and comparison with targets and other districts decides where detection crews go first.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for step testing a district to locate a leak area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one night step test in a district with high night flow.

cards.label: Plan the valve sequence that will close the district in sections, smallest area last
Notify dispatch and record the starting district night flow
Close the first section valve and record the drop in inlet flow
Continue closing sections in sequence, recording the flow drop at each step
Identify the section with the largest unexplained flow drop
Reopen all valves in reverse order and mark the suspect section for leak sounding

tasks.explanation: Each valve closure removes one section from supply, so the flow drop belongs to that section. The largest unexplained drop points to the leak area, and reopening in reverse restores supply in a controlled order.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a leak sounding survey of a high loss district.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: sounding of all fittings in one district.

cards.label: Divide the district into sounding routes that cover every valve and hydrant
Brief the crew on listening equipment use and the recording sheet
Sound each fitting and mark any leak noise with its strength
Correlate or pinpoint the strongest noises to locate the leak position
Raise repair work orders for confirmed leak locations
Resound the district after repairs to confirm the noise is gone

tasks.explanation: Complete coverage prevents missed leaks between fittings. Marked noise strength guides correlation effort, repairs follow confirmed locations, and resounding proves the work reduced loss rather than assuming it did.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a large meter accuracy testing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual testing of large customer meters.

cards.label: Rank large meters by consumption so the biggest users are tested first
Notify each customer and book the test visit
Test the meter at low, medium and high flows and record accuracy at each
Compare results with the utility accuracy limits
Repair, recalibrate or replace meters outside the limits
Update the billing adjustment and the meter record from the test results

tasks.explanation: Testing the largest meters first protects the most revenue and the water balance. Accuracy across the flow range matters because a meter can pass at high flow and fail at low flow, and records plus billing are corrected from the same results.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the annual system water balance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one calendar year water balance for the whole system.

cards.label: Total the treated water supplied into the distribution system
Total billed metered and billed unmetered consumption
Estimate unbilled authorized use such as flushing and fire fighting
Apply meter accuracy and data handling adjustments from test records
Calculate non revenue water and its main components
Present the balance and the largest loss component to management

tasks.explanation: The balance starts from measured supply and consumption before any estimates are added. Separating authorized unbilled use and adjustments from real losses shows whether the biggest problem is leakage, metering or data, which decides the control program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for investigating apparent losses in the water balance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a review triggered by rising non revenue water with stable night flows.

cards.label: Confirm production meter readings and check for data transfer errors
Review large meter test results for under registration
Check for unbilled accounts and inactive accounts still taking water
Review estimates used for unread meters in the billing system
Correct the data or metering fault found
Recalculate the water balance and report the change to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Stable night flows with rising non revenue water point to apparent rather than real losses. The review works through metering, billing and data causes in order, corrects the fault, and proves the effect by recalculating the balance.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps when unauthorized hydrant use is found during a loss survey.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one site where a tanker is filling without a permit.

cards.label: Record the hydrant, time, vehicle and estimated filling rate from a safe position
Check the permit records to confirm no hydrant use permit covers the site
Notify the supervisor and the bylaw contact used by the utility
Direct the user to stop and to the permit and metered filling process
Estimate the volume taken for the water balance records
Inspect the hydrant and backflow risk and record the findings

tasks.explanation: Evidence is recorded before any confrontation, and the permit check confirms the use is unauthorized. Stopping the use protects revenue and water quality, the volume estimate keeps the water balance honest, and the hydrant is checked for damage or contamination risk.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for verifying water loss savings after a leak repair program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one district where several leaks were repaired last month.

cards.label: Confirm all repair work orders in the district are closed with locations recorded
Download the district night flow data for the weeks after the repairs
Compare the new minimum night flow with the pre repair baseline
Convert the flow reduction to a daily leakage saving
Check that pressures in the district remain in the target range
Report the verified saving and update the district loss ranking

tasks.explanation: Savings are claimed only from measured night flow change against the pre repair baseline. Pressure is checked so a saving is not just customers receiving less water, and the updated ranking sends the next effort to the district that now needs it most.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual water loss program review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: yearly review covering all districts and programs.

cards.label: Compile district night flow and leakage rankings for the year
Total leaks found and repaired by detection method
Review meter testing results and apparent loss corrections
Compare total non revenue water with the previous year and the target
Rank next year work by the largest remaining loss volumes
Present the review and the proposed program to management for approval

tasks.explanation: The annual review ranks districts and methods by measured results, not by habit. Comparing the balance year to year shows whether the program is working, and ranking next year work by remaining volume keeps effort on the biggest losses.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing a chlorine residual management program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program design for the whole distribution system.

cards.label: Map sampling points that represent sources, storage outlets and far ends
Review a year of residual results to find low residual areas and seasons
Set target residual ranges for inlets, mid system and far ends
Assign monitoring frequencies for each class of sampling point
Define the response actions for results below the target range
Approve the program and train the sampling and operations staff

tasks.explanation: Representative points and a year of history show where and when residuals fail. Targets by location make results judgeable, defined responses prevent ad hoc decisions, and training makes the program work the same on every shift.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a nitrification monitoring round in a chloraminated storage area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one round at a tank outlet and nearby distribution sites. Use only where the system uses chloramines.

cards.label: Select sites at the tank outlet, a nearby dead end and a mid area control point
Measure total chlorine, free ammonia and nitrite at each site in that order of collection
Compare results with the utility action levels for nitrification signs
Check tank turnover and water age for the same period
Increase flushing or turnover at sites showing early nitrification signs
Record the round and schedule the follow up round sooner than routine

tasks.explanation: Nitrification is tracked by the pattern across total chlorine, free ammonia and nitrite together, not by one result alone. Comparing sites separates a tank problem from a local dead end problem, and early action plus closer follow up stops a full episode.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for responding to confirmed nitrification in a storage tank.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one tank with falling total chlorine and rising nitrite.

cards.label: Confirm the result with repeat samples at the tank outlet and in the tank area
Review tank levels and turnover to find the water age driving the episode
Increase tank turnover by adjusting operating levels and cycling the tank
Flush the distribution area fed by the tank, starting nearest the tank
Retest total chlorine and nitrite until results return to normal range
Document the episode, the cause found and the actions taken

tasks.explanation: Repeat samples confirm the episode before major action. Turnover addresses the root cause, which is old water, flushing refreshes the affected area from the tank outward, and retesting proves recovery before the episode is closed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for triaging water quality complaints at the program level each morning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the daily review of complaints received in the last day.

cards.label: List all taste, odour, colour and pressure complaints with addresses and times
Plot the addresses to check for clustering by area, main or tank zone
Compare clusters with recent flushing, breaks and tank operations
Assign site visits starting with any cluster that suggests a system cause
Give single isolated complaints the standard customer guidance and a callback
Record the triage decisions and any pattern carried to the weekly review

tasks.explanation: Daily triage separates isolated customer plumbing issues from early signs of a system event. Clusters are checked against operations first because timing often explains them, and recording patterns daily lets the weekly review see trends no single day shows.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the annual distribution sampling schedule.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: schedule for bacteriological and chemical sampling under provincial drinking water requirements.

cards.label: List the sample types, counts and locations required by the provincial program
Spread samples evenly across weeks so no month is overloaded or missed
Assign sites so far ends, dead ends and storage outlets are all represented
Build in repeat and follow up sample capacity for adverse results
Issue the schedule to samplers with site access notes
Track completion weekly and reschedule any missed sample within its window

tasks.explanation: The schedule starts from the required counts and locations, then spreads work so compliance does not depend on one busy week. Follow up capacity is planned rather than improvised, and weekly tracking catches a missed sample while it can still be taken in its window.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps in the program response to an adverse bacteriological result in distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one adverse result at a routine distribution site, following provincial drinking water requirements.

cards.label: Confirm the result details with the laboratory and record the site and time
Notify the supervisor and the provincial contact as the utility procedure requires
Collect repeat samples at the site, upstream and downstream as directed
Flush the area around the site if directed while samples are pending
Review results and lift any advisory only when the procedure criteria are met
Complete the adverse result report and file the full record

tasks.explanation: Adverse results follow the set procedure without improvisation: confirmation and notification first, then the directed resampling pattern that locates the extent, and closure only when the criteria in the procedure are met and documented.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a dead end water quality improvement program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all dead ends in the system ranked for action.

cards.label: Inventory dead ends from the map and record main size and customer count for each
Rank dead ends by residual history, complaints and water age
Choose the remedy for each, such as routine flushing, an auto flusher or looping
Install or schedule the chosen remedy for the highest ranked dead ends first
Monitor residuals at treated dead ends for one season
Report which remedies held residuals in range and adjust the program

tasks.explanation: Dead ends are ranked by measured quality, not by complaint volume alone. Remedies match the severity at each site, monitoring over a season proves which remedies work in this system, and the program is adjusted from that evidence.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for assessing mixing in a ground storage reservoir.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one reservoir suspected of stratification and old water pockets.

cards.label: Review inlet and outlet locations and the normal fill and draw pattern
Collect temperature and residual samples at different depths or ports
Compare depth results to confirm whether stratification is present
Evaluate a mixer or inlet change against the stratification found
Install the selected measure and repeat the depth sampling
Record whether residuals equalized and set the routine check interval

tasks.explanation: Stratification must be proven by depth sampling before money is spent on mixing. The fill pattern explains the cause, the chosen measure is verified by repeating the same sampling, and a routine interval keeps the fix monitored.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing a booster chlorination station performance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one booster station feeding a far end area.

cards.label: Compare residuals upstream and downstream of the booster station
Review the booster feed records and chemical use for the period
Check the feed equipment, injection point and residual analyser calibration
Adjust the dose setpoint only if equipment and calibration are sound
Monitor downstream far end residuals for the following week
Record the review and the setpoint in the station log

tasks.explanation: Upstream and downstream residuals show what the booster is actually adding. Equipment and analyser faults are ruled out before the dose is changed, because adjusting a dose to match a faulty analyser makes control worse, and a week of far end results proves the change.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the annual water quality program report.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual report covering residuals, complaints, sampling and flushing.

cards.label: Compile residual compliance results by area and season
Summarize complaints by type and area and compare with last year
Summarize sampling completion and any adverse results and responses
Summarize flushing volumes and the areas flushed
Identify the areas and seasons needing program changes next year
Present the report to management and file it with the program records

tasks.explanation: The annual report combines residuals, complaints, sampling and flushing so patterns that cross programs become visible. Areas and seasons needing change are identified from the combined evidence, which is what makes next year program better rather than just repeated.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing flushing zones for a system wide unidirectional flushing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: zone design stage for the whole system.

cards.label: Review the system map, source locations and historical complaint and residual data
Divide the system into zones that can each be fed from a single inlet
Sequence zones so work starts at the sources and moves outward
List the valves and hydrants to be used in each zone in operating order
Estimate water needs and crew time for each zone
Approve the zone plan before any customer notices are issued

tasks.explanation: Zones must each work from one inlet or the flow will not be unidirectional. Sequencing from the sources outward protects cleaned mains, the valve and hydrant list is the field plan, and approval comes before public notice so the promise matches the plan.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing a flushing sequence to reach target velocity in a large main.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one large diameter main segment in a flushing zone.

cards.label: Confirm the main size, length and the hydrants available for the segment
Select the hydrant combination that gives the target flushing velocity
Sequence intermediate valves so flow passes through the segment in one direction
Plan the discharge route and erosion controls for the chosen hydrants
Brief the crew on the opening order and the clarity and residual targets
Record the achieved flow and whether the segment ran clear

tasks.explanation: Velocity comes from the hydrant combination matched to the main size, so selection precedes valve work. Discharge is planned before high flow starts, and recording achieved flow shows whether the design velocity was truly reached.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing customer notices for a flushing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: notices for one zone scheduled next week.

cards.label: Confirm the zone dates and the daily work areas from the approved plan
Draft the notice with dates, possible discolouration advice and a contact number
Deliver notices to the zone in the order the streets will be flushed
Post the zone schedule on the utility public notice channel
Brief dispatch and customer service on the schedule and the standard advice
Keep a delivery record so any complaint can be checked against notice coverage

tasks.explanation: Notices follow the approved dates, never precede them. Delivery in flushing order means each street is warned just before its work, dispatch shares the same schedule, and the delivery record answers later questions about who was warned.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning a swabbing run for a tuberculated main.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one main selected for foam swab cleaning.

cards.label: Confirm from records and flushing results that deposits need swabbing, not flushing alone
Select launch and retrieval points and the valves for isolating the run
Notify affected customers and plan the outage window
Stage swabs, launch gear and discharge controls at the launch point
Plan the post run flushing, disinfection checks and sampling
Approve the run plan with the supervisor before the outage is booked

tasks.explanation: Swabbing is chosen only when flushing has proven insufficient. Isolation points and the outage are planned before customers are notified, post run flushing and sampling are part of the same plan, and approval precedes booking the outage.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for placing automatic flushers on chronic low residual dead ends.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: placement program for auto flushers across the system.

cards.label: Rank dead ends by how often residuals fall below target despite manual flushing
Check each candidate site for drainage, power or battery access and winter protection
Set the flush frequency and duration from the water age at the site
Install the unit and set its controller to the planned program
Measure residuals at the site over the first month and adjust the program
Add the unit to the inspection route and record its settings

tasks.explanation: Auto flushers go where manual flushing has already failed to hold residuals, so the ranking is evidence based. Drainage and winter protection decide whether a site can work at all in a western Canadian winter, and first month residuals prove the settings.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for tracking water used by the flushing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: tracking setup for one flushing season.

cards.label: Define how each flush type will have its volume estimated or metered
Issue the field sheet that records hydrant, time open and estimated flow
Collect sheets weekly and total volumes by zone
Compare flushing volumes with the water balance unbilled authorized use
Investigate any zone where recorded use and estimates differ widely
Report season totals and unit volumes per main length to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Consistent estimation methods make zone totals comparable. Weekly collection catches missing sheets while crews remember the work, comparison with the water balance validates the method, and reporting per length shows where flushing effort is concentrated.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing whether a flushing program improved water quality.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review one season after a full system program.

cards.label: Compile residual results from before and after the program by area
Compare complaint counts for discolouration and taste for the same periods
Review the volumes used and the time each zone took
Identify areas where quality did not improve despite flushing
Recommend repeat flushing, swabbing or main renewal for those areas
Present the effectiveness review and recommendations to management

tasks.explanation: Effectiveness is judged by quality change, not by volumes flushed. Areas that did not improve need a different remedy, and the review names it, so the next program is designed from results rather than repeated by habit.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adapting the flushing program for winter operation.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: winter version of the routine flushing round in a northern prairie system.

cards.label: Identify flushing points that can discharge without creating ice hazards on roads and walks
Reduce flush durations to the minimum that still reaches clarity and residual targets
Schedule winter flushes for the warmest part of the day where practical
Fit discharge controls that spread water to avoid a single icing point
Check each hydrant drains fully after its winter flush
Record winter results separately so spring planning sees the winter pattern

tasks.explanation: Winter flushing trades a little duration for safety, because discharge ice is a public hazard and a liability. Drainage checks matter more in winter, since a hydrant left holding water can freeze and split, and separate records keep winter limits visible in planning.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adding newly constructed mains to the flushing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: new mains accepted into the system this year.

cards.label: Collect the as built records and valve and hydrant lists for each new main
Identify new dead ends and low turnover sections created by the construction
Add the new points to the flushing routes in the correct outward sequence
Set initial flushing frequencies from the expected water age
Measure residuals at the new points during the first season
Adjust frequencies and update the program map at season end

tasks.explanation: New mains change water age patterns, so they enter the program from their as built records, not from memory. Initial frequencies are set from expected age, first season residuals test that estimate, and the map is corrected at season end.
